answer.label: Written by

answer.sourceLine: Genuinely Aristotle, from the ‘Politics’, Book I, chapter 2 (Bekker 1253a31). This exact wording is Benjamin Jowett’s celebrated 1885 English translation (Oxford, Clarendon Press) — confirmed word-for-word against the Jowett text ↗ and cross-checked against the Greek in the Perseus edition ↗.

source.heading: The source
source.excerpt: For man, when perfected, is the best of animals, but, when separated from law and justice, he is the worst of all; since armed injustice is the more dangerous, and he is equipped at birth with the arms of intelligence and with moral qualities which he may use for the worst ends. Wherefore, if he have not virtue, he is the most unholy and the most savage of animals, and the most full of lust and gluttony. But justice is the bond of men in states.
trail: The line is genuinely Aristotle: it appears in the Politics, Book I, ch. 2 ↗, in Benjamin Jowett’s translation, with this exact wording.
The Greek passage (Bekker 1253a31) is confirmed in the Perseus Digital Library ↗, where H. Rackham renders it “the worst of all when sundered from law and justice.”
Jowett’s translation was first published in 1885 ↗ by the Clarendon Press, Oxford — the source of the wording that circulates today.
source.excerptNote: From Aristotle’s argument that man is by nature a ‘political animal’ whose capacities for reason and speech make him best under law — and most dangerous without it.

author.bio: Aristotle of Stagira (384–322 BC) was a Greek philosopher and polymath whose works span logic, ethics, biology, metaphysics, rhetoric and politics. His Politics examines the city-state (polis) as the natural community in which humans flourish, arguing that man is by nature a ‘political animal’ who realizes his full nature only under law and justice.

misattribution.heading: Correctly Aristotle — but often misquoted
misattribution.intro: The attribution here is right: this is real Aristotle. What gets garbled is the wording — the internet circulates several looser paraphrases alongside the genuine Jowett line.

items.who: “At his best, man is the noblest of all animals; separated from law and justice, he is the worst.”
items.why: This popular short form — spread by sites like BrainyQuote ↗ — is a loose paraphrase, not any standard published translation. Jowett’s actual text reads “when perfected, is the best of animals… the worst of all.”

items.who: “For as man is the best of the animals when perfected, so he is the worst of all when sundered from law and justice.”
items.why: This is H. Rackham’s Loeb rendering, seen in the Perseus edition ↗ — the same passage, different wording.

misattribution.truthLine: The thought and the source are authentically Aristotle’s; the familiar “when perfected… worst of all” phrasing is Benjamin Jowett’s 1885 translation of the Politics, Book I ↗.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The line closes Aristotle’s argument in Politics Book I that the city-state (polis) exists by nature and that “man is by nature a political animal.” Because humans alone possess reasoned speech (logos) — the ability to declare the just and the unjust — they are uniquely fitted for life under law.

That same faculty is double-edged: intelligence and appetite “equipped at birth” can serve virtue or, unchecked by law and justice, the worst ends. Hence Aristotle’s conclusion that justice is “the bond of men in states.”
context.pull: Justice is the bond of men in states.
